To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) female zebra finch hematological parameters are reduced during egg production, (2) the reduction in hematological parameters is not due to resource availability but rather due to suppression of erythropoeisis, (3) the reduction in red blood cell counts is not due to hemodilution but rather due to a decrease in red blood cell volume.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the anemia associated with reproductive investment in egg laying is due to hemodilution (i.e. increased plasma volume) associated with egg production, but is modulated by a transient suppression of erythroid production, which is followed by an increase in the production and release of reticulocytic cells.

the mechanism of anemia associated to egg production in zebra finches is not due to hemodilution, but is due to a transient suppression of erythopoiesis, and this suppression is independent of diet quality.
egg-laying females show a transient suppression of erythroid production that is not associated with a lack of resources.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
reproductive anemia is not a resource-dependent response to egg production, but rather a direct consequence of the physiological demands of egg production on erythropoieses.

the mechanisms underlying reproductive anemias in egg-laying birds are not resource dependent and, in addition to the well-documented hemodilution effects, are also associated with suppression of erythropoesis and subsequent increased reticulocyte production.

egg-laying females are anemic due to a suppression of erythropoesis, which is associated with a decrease in the number of red blood cells in the circulation, a decrease in the hemoglobin concentration of the plasma, and an increase in the number of immature red blood cells in circulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the hematological changes associated with reproduction in birds are not simply due to a reduction in erythropoietic drive, but rather to a complex interplay between the production and release of immature red blood cells and the rate of clearance of senescent cells from the circulation.
